title: Rahab in Jericho
lead: Neither your past nor your background shuts you out of God’s future.
questions: Whom have you written off from God’s future because of their past?
Which of the people “in the wall” might put you to shame with their faith today, if you let them speak?
Are you living inside some wall yourself, and what is your scarlet cord: today’s decision of faith, not yesterday’s life story?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Forty years after the report that cost a whole generation of Israel their lives, Joshua sends two spies into Jericho. They end up at the house of Rahab, a prostitute who lived in the city wall itself. That was the cheapest place to live, home to the most shameful trades. A woman, a Canaanite, a prostitute: excluded three times over. The story of salvation has a strange habit of entering cities through doors exactly like that.

She is the one who tells them the thing that got this story into the Bible: “I know that the LORD has given you this land and that the fear of you has fallen on us.” Forty years earlier the spies had felt like grasshoppers beside the Canaanites; Rahab tells them how it really was: ever since God’s people crossed the sea, it was Canaan that had been trembling. And then she confesses: “the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below.” She hadn’t seen a single plague, or the sea, or the manna. She had heard the same news as all of Jericho. The difference was that the city was only afraid, and she believed. Faith isn’t born from the amount of evidence, but from what a person does with the news that reaches them.

The sign of her rescue was a scarlet cord in the window. Interestingly, the Hebrew word tiqwah, which almost everywhere else means “hope” or “expectation,” in this story means precisely a cord. It’s hard to imagine a more vivid picture: Rahab’s hope was, in a sense, hung in the window. We know the terms of the agreement from Egypt: a sign on the house, the family gathered inside, no one allowed out. This is Passover in Jericho. What saved people wasn’t background or merit but staying inside the house marked with the scarlet cord; once again the line ran not between nations but between those who believed and those who didn’t. Out of the whole city, one house was saved. Rahab “has lived among the Israelites to this day,” and the New Testament opens with a genealogy in which we read: “Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab.” The prostitute from the wall of Jericho became the great-great-grandmother of David and an ancestor of the Messiah. Scripture never once whitewashes her life. It shows what grace does with life stories that can’t be retouched.

This story asks us an uncomfortable question: whom do we consider a Rahab? Who, in our eyes, lives in the wall, with a past that rules them out in advance? In a city full of news about God, the one who believed was the one nobody expected. People from the walls are sometimes closer to the Kingdom than people in church.

Forty years have passed since the report that cost a whole generation of Israel their lives. The new leader, Joshua, was once a spy himself. Before crossing the Jordan he also sends out spies, but this time he learns from past mistakes: two men instead of twelve, in secret instead of in public, and no assembly called to hear the report. The story in Joshua 2 is built exactly like the one in Numbers: sending, entering, returning, reporting. Except this time everything goes the other way. And the most valuable thing the spies bring back from Jericho isn’t information but a person. In this section on faith in the minority, this story has a special place: yesterday the minority was a handful of faithful people in the middle of God’s people; today it is one believing person in a city that knew about the God of Israel only as much as rumor had brought. It turns out that the minority of faith has no lower limit. One woman in a window is enough.

sections.heading: A House in the Wall
paragraphs: “So they went and entered the house of a prostitute named Rahab and stayed there.” The text doesn’t sugarcoat anything, and neither should we. Rahab was a prostitute, and her house stood in the city wall itself, on the outer edge of Jericho. Housing there was the cheapest, home to the most shameful trades. A house like that usually doubled as an inn, which is why two strangers could stay there without immediately raising suspicion. If you were looking for the person at the very bottom of the ladder in this doomed city, it would be her: a woman, a Canaanite, a prostitute, a resident of the wall. Excluded three times over: by gender, by origin, and by occupation. The story of salvation has a strange habit of entering cities through doors exactly like that.

sections.heading: A Confession from Behind the Wall
paragraphs: When the king’s messengers show up with orders to hand over the spies, Rahab hides the men on her roof, and that night she tells them the thing that got this story into the Bible: “I know that the LORD has given you this land and that the fear of you has fallen on us, so that all who dwell in the land are melting in fear of you. For we have heard how the LORD dried up the waters of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt.” Set that sentence beside the report from forty years before. Those spies came back convinced that the Canaanites saw them as grasshoppers. Rahab, a Canaanite, says that Jericho was gripped by fear of Israel because of the news of the parted sea and the victories that followed. Her words show that the picture of the Canaanites painted by the earlier spies was not a true assessment of the situation. And then comes a confession no one in Israel would have been ashamed of: “the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below.” That is almost word for word a sentence from a speech of Moses. Where did she get it? She hadn’t seen a single plague, or the split sea, or the manna. She had heard. The same news was going around Jericho, and that is why the whole city was afraid. She alone decided to believe. Faith isn’t born from the amount of evidence, but from what a person does with the news that reaches them. In a whole city full of information about God, one person believed, and it was someone nobody would have bet on. Real faith isn’t knowing the facts; it is trusting that in spite of everything, God can save me.

There is one more thing in her words we mustn’t pass by: the sea she talks about had parted forty years earlier. That news was still alive in Jericho after all those years. The text doesn’t say when exactly Rahab heard it, or how long faith had been growing in her. The Almighty led Israel through the wilderness for forty years, and during that time, in Jericho, the faith of one woman nobody in Israel knew about was quietly ripening. We never know in whom some news about God, heard years ago, is at work. Sometimes what looks like a city locked up tight has one window that has been waiting a long time for a cord.

sections.heading: Faith with Ethics Under Construction
paragraphs: Honesty requires us to notice something uncomfortable in this story, too: Rahab lied to the king’s men. She said the spies had left, when they were lying hidden under stalks of flax on her roof. The Bible neither praises nor condemns this lie; it simply records it. And when the New Testament twice holds Rahab up as an example, it praises her faith and her action, welcoming the messengers and saving them, not the technique she used to do it. That is an important lesson about how faith begins: Rahab came to believe in the LORD with a morality shaped by Jericho and by her trade. Her faith was real before her life had time to get in order. God accepts people whose ethics are still under construction, and He doesn’t make them grow up into holiness first before they can begin. If He had waited until Rahab was beyond reproach, Jericho would have fallen with her in it.

sections.heading: A Cord Called Hope
paragraphs: Rahab asks for an oath: since I showed you kindness, show kindness to my family. Spare my father, my mother, my brothers and sisters. The spies agree and set a sign: “you have tied this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down.” And right here the Hebrew text hides a remarkable detail. The word tiqwah, used for this cord, means “hope” or “expectation” in dozens of other places in the Hebrew Bible. Only here, in Rahab’s story, is the same word used for a physical cord hung in a window. No one translates this sentence “tie hope to the window.” Here tiqwah really does mean a cord. But it’s hard not to see the remarkable picture the Hebrew text creates: Rahab’s hope is hanging in the window of her house. Her life and the life of her whole family depend on that sign. The series you are reading could have taken its title from this one verse.

sections.heading: Passover in Jericho
paragraphs: Look at the terms of the agreement, because we’ve seen them somewhere before: a sign in red thread on the house; the whole family gathered inside; “If anyone goes out the door of your house into the street, his blood will be on his own head”; rescue for everyone who stays in the marked place. This is Passover. The same logic that protected the houses marked with the lamb’s blood in Egypt is now at work in Jericho, in the house of a Canaanite prostitute: what saves is not background or merit, but staying in the house with the scarlet cord. In Egypt the line didn’t run between one nation and another. It ran between those who believed and those who didn’t, and here it is the same. Out of the whole city devoted to destruction, one family was saved: the ones who believed the warning and took shelter in the designated place. God doesn’t change the rules, even when the side of the wall changes.

It’s also worth measuring how long this faith had to last. The cord went up in the window the day the spies left, but Jericho fell only after the crossing of the Jordan and after seven days of a strange siege, in which the army just marched around the walls in silence. Through all those days Rahab kept her whole family in her small house and watched from the window an army that was acting very strangely. She had to explain to her father and brothers why they should sit in a prostitute’s house instead of defending the city. Faith is rarely one brave evening. More often it is a cord that stays hanging in the window long after the decision was made, a cord you must not take down.

sections.heading: She Lived Among Israel
paragraphs: When Jericho fell, Joshua sent the same two spies: “Go into the house of the prostitute and bring out the woman and all who are with her.” They rescued Rahab, her parents, her brothers, and everything she had. And then the narrator recorded the sentence that is this story’s quiet triumph: “So she has lived among the Israelites to this day.” The woman from the wall of Jericho came into the heart of God’s people and stayed. But the Bible doesn’t stop there. Centuries later, on the first page of the New Testament, in Jesus’ genealogy, we read: “Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab, Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, Obed the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David the king.” Rahab married in Israel and became the great-great-grandmother of King David, and so an ancestor of the Messiah. In Jesus’ genealogy Matthew names four women from long ago, and all four have stories that polite company tells in a whisper: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth the Moabite, and Uriah’s wife. Before Jesus says a single word of the gospel, His own family tree already proclaims that in God’s family there is room for people with a past and for outsiders. And the New Testament writers would come back to Rahab twice more: as an example of faith and as an example of deeds. The woman her city was ashamed of became, in Scripture, a model of both at once. And nobody in those texts tries to clean up her record: every time, the same word stands next to her name, prostitute, as if Scripture wanted to make sure no one would miss whom God had written into the family. The Bible doesn’t whitewash the lives of its heroes. It shows what grace does with life stories that can’t be retouched.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: This story asks the community of believers one uncomfortable question: whom do we consider a Rahab? Who lives in the wall of our town, with a life story told in whispers, with a job, a background, or a past that in our eyes rules them out in advance? Jericho was full of people more respectable than Rahab. She was the one saved, because faith doesn’t ask about your life story so far, only about today’s decision. God didn’t just forgive her. He wrote her into His Son’s family tree, on the very first page of the New Testament, alongside patriarchs and kings. If you carry the conviction that your past or your background has put you on the wrong side of the wall for good, read again what the cord in her window was called. And if you’ve been part of the community forever and your record is clean, remember one thing from this story: in a city full of news about God, the only one who believed was the one nobody expected. People from the walls are sometimes closer to the Kingdom than people from the town square.
